title: Blizzard doing 'a thorough scrub' of illegitimate World of Warcraft Mythic-Plus dungeon rankings, with more changes to come
text:
Blizzard is scrubbing through its new World of Warcraft Mythic Plus Dungeon top-1% rankings for people who paid for carries, World of Warcraft game director Ion Hazzikostas says.
The timed dungeon mode offered its first-ever rewards at that level this past season in the Midnight expansion, which ended August 11. Unlike similar high-end rewards in PvP combat, this ranking level in Mythic Plus dungeons was a flat percentage of players, rather than a set score they had to achieve.
Some players paid for the privilege, and the glowy red-and-black bird mount that came with the title. These boosts were particularly controversial, as the percentage cutoff meant that every successful carry removed a player that legitimately earned the score.
"The team is doing a thorough scrub of this for Season 1 and will share more with the community soon about how we approached that review, as well as the final results," Hazzikostas said.
A constant grind to keep a reward in sight
"I hit 1% M+ rating yesterday and it lasted for 5 minutes," wrote one typical person on Reddit just before the end of the season. "The 1% cutoff is going up by about 2 points every day. Ninety percent of +21 [level] groups in the group finder are 'note' keys where you need to pay the keyholder to be invited. People are also buying actual boosts en masse because of the new 1% title and resilient keystones making it possible. Playing organically is no longer possible."
The 1% rewards have not yet been awarded in game. Hazzikostas and associate game director Paul Kubit said they are popular and will continue.
Blizzard recently removed the Mythic raiding mount from the accounts of players determined to have paid for them in the game's large-group content, primarily with real-money transactions, which are forbidden by WoW's terms of service.
Carries paid only in gold to specific guilds or individuals appear to be legitimate , based on past Blizzard posts and enforcement actions, but some players caught by the corrective wave in raids say they paid in gold and had their mounts removed anyway. (That's happened in the past when the sellers who got people a ranking or reward took in-game gold in some cases and real money in others, or when cross-server boosting communities were involved.)
Sales are not the only part of the new Mythic Plus rewards that players are heatedly discussing. The decision to make the cutoff a percentage rather than a fixed rating means that people near the cutoff had to play nearly continuously at the end of their season to keep their ranking.
A percentage cutoff to keep things exciting—but did it work?
Kubit, who is in charge of the Midnight expansion, said making the cutoff percentage-based keeps people playing even as their numbers increase over the course of a season.
"This is aimed at the 1%, which is by definition pretty elite, one of those people who really like to push the upper end of what mythic plus gameplay is all about," he says. "We want to make sure that you do truly feel like you can do that, as opposed to laying off the gas."
Numbers suggest that goal may not have entirely played out as expected, however. Raider.io , which tracks Mythic Plus Dungeon statistics, shows that more people played Mythic Plus dungeons at the start and end of Midnight's first season than did the first season in The War Within expansion (about 5.2 million, compared to about 2.5 million), but the drop-off at the end of the season was actually steeper in Midnight than it was in War Within.
Just 12.3% of players were still doing the dungeons at the end of Midnight Season 1, versus 16.8% in War Within. Those numbers of players remained fairly static for the six weeks at the end of both seasons.
Players enthusiastic about a new reward, but mixed on how it was awarded
Players' reactions were decidedly mixed.
"That uncertainty makes the end of the season feel more stressful than exciting," said one typical poster on Reddit.
"The reason a percentile is used is because it correlates with season difficulty. In this particular case 3900 is feasible this season but may not be feasible in others," countered another in the same post.
The addition of "resilient" keys, which don't drop in level once you've completed that difficulty in all available dungeons, has made pushing ever-higher levels—and selling those timed dungeons—easier.
Player versus player rewards were initially based on percentage, as well, near when World of Warcraft first launched. In the Burning Crusade, the top .5% of PvP arena players were awarded Elite mounts. After players complaints about the grind and rampant sales, that was changed to a fixed rating in the Mists of Pandaria expansion, then eventually to the modern system, which requires a fixed rating plus a number of wins above that rating, to help keep the number of sales down.
(Image credit: Blizzard Entertainment) Class balance makes earning the bird tougher for some players
The composition of groups that are successfully timing Mythic Plus dungeons has also become more homogenized than ever before. While Raider.io charts show a broad variety of the 40 possible character classes and specializations, the vast majority of Mythic Plus keys over level 20 (required for the 1% title) contain some combination of the same seven "meta" specs in each five-player group: guardian druid, unholy death knight, devourer demon hunter, mistweaver monk, augmentation evoker, restoration shaman and retribution paladin.
You shouldn't feel forced into any particular meta spec.
Paul Kubit, associate game director
The top tank specialization, guardian druid, was seen 518,467 times in dungeons recorded on Raider.io at that level over the course of the season. The bottom tank, blood death knight, was seen 7,635. Since many keys are run over and over again by the same players, that boils down to an even tinier number of players who actually completed dungeons at this level.
"When we're thinking about world record folks, then some of the fun of that gameplay is identifying, 'What if I switch to this character in this particular spec, and solve the puzzle that way?' But when you get closer to the 1%, ideally for anyone there, we want you to play the classes and specs that you like playing, that you feel like you're good at," Kubit says. "You shouldn't feel forced into any particular meta spec."
"Obviously players are going to gravitate toward certain specs when we're talking about the 1%," says Andrew De Souza, lead encounter designer. "Ninety-nine percent of players are able to get to Keystone Myth [3400 rating, compared to about 4000 for the top 1%] with any given comp."
Dungeons are designed for all classes to play, but 1% mounts may get more specific
They do watch dungeons to make sure they don't require a specific class, he says.
"In some cases that's going to naturally fit—poisons and curses in Altar of Fangs [dungeon], that's probably going to lean towards [having] a shaman," he says. "We are saying okay, but what if there's not a shaman? What does this pack look like? So we're absolutely making those considerations. It's okay if this class dunks on this trash mob. They're allowed to be awesome here—just within reason. We are trying to serve the largest audience possible."
Blizzard is now figuring out how to implement specialization-specific 1% cutoffs, Hazzikostas says, though it won't be this season—Season 2 just began—and the details remain to be hammered out (including, for example, whether it would still be the top 1% in that scenario). He mentioned the possibility in an interview with PsyBear that ran earlier this week, then kept an eye on the discussion.
"While the spec-specific title reward is something we're excited to explore," he tells us, "there are still a number of logistics, factors, and scenarios we'll need to account for as we build out that capability, to ensure fairness across the board. But it seems from our initial discussion of this idea that this is something the community is equally excited about, so we'll share more when we can."

title: After the debacle of Cyberpunk 2077, CD Projekt says The Witcher 4 is already running on PC and consoles, promises 'it's going to run' on all target platforms
text:
Cyberpunk 2077 now is one of the best RPGs money can buy. But Cyberpunk 2077 then , which is to say when it was new, was not. It was pretty okay on PC , aside from a horde of bugs, but it was such a performance catastrophe on the PlayStation 4 that Sony literally booted it off the PlayStation Store . Even when it was allowed back in the building six months later, Sony slapped a notice on it warning people that it was still potentially dodgy .
Speaking to Game Developer , CD Projekt Red co-CEO Michał Nowakowski said that failure arose from the studio's ambitions for the game, which led it to develop on PC first. "We want[ed] to push the boundaries of what is doable in terms of cinematic feeling and whatnot [in Cyberpunk 2077], and PC was just the best suited rig for that," Nowakowski said. "There was this, as it turned out, false belief that toning it down to whatever was the current gen is not going to be that much of a challenge."
There was also a little bit of belief in a Polish take on the ol' Bioware magic : Nowakowski said the studio "got a bit lucky here and there" with The Witcher 3, leading it to believe that Cyberpunk would ultimately be fine too.
Of course, Cyberpunk 2077 was most definitely not fine, and with that humiliation firmly burned into its collective consciousness, CD Projekt Red is approaching The Witcher 4 with a little more care and consideration to ensure the new game runs properly on all platforms it's coming to. If development hits a snag on any single platform, for instance, the studio stops to fix it rather than simply pressing ahead and coming back to clean it up later.
"For example, technically, we should hit, let's say, 10 checkmarks," Nowakowski said. "Back in the past, if we missed one or two, we were like, 'we're gonna catch up with that later on.' Sometimes we did, but sometimes we didn't, and then two milestones or three milestones down the road, you have like four or five missing checkmarks and it's not that easy."
The net result is parity right from the get-go: "You come to the studio, you launch Witcher 4 right now. You can launch it on PC. You can launch it on PS5. You can launch it on Xbox Series X, and it's going to run," Nowakowski said.
'We're doing our best to ensure our game runs' is a low bar, sure, but given how poorly Cyberpunk 2077 went at launch it's not surprising that CD Projekt is making the point—and so, here's hoping it's able to pull it off. The Witcher 4 still doesn't have a release date (and probably won't for a good long time yet) but is currently "targeting" a 2028 release .

title: One of Elden Ring's top sleuths has already unmasked its new DLC characters
text:
Longtime FromSoftware dataminer Zullie the Witch has come out with a new video showing off the close-up details of Elden Ring's two new NPC invaders. Knight Leontiel and Noble Broken Mask were both added to the game as part of Elden Ring's Tarnished Edition DLC.
Knight Leontiel is a straight "hey, I know them" reference to Lucatiel of Mirrah from Dark Souls 2, boasting an HD remaster of her signature conquistador fit and nimble greatsword. Take off the mask, though, and Leontiel practically is Lucatiel, even down to a burn mark over her left eye that corresponds to the hollowing rot Lucatiel suffered in Dark Souls 2.
Noble Broken Mask, meanwhile, may obliquely give us a better idea of what his base game counterpart and spiritual rival, Goldmask, is supposed to look like. Goldmask's model has a face, but it seems like a generic placeholder element. Broken Mask has an austere, pinched face with striking pale gold eyes, and Zullie points out that he bears a more than passing resemblance to the typically obscured faces of Elden Ring's perfumer enemies.
Zullie provides character creation slider information for the two so you can perfectly recreate either one as your own guy⁠—most FromSoft NPCs are made using the same tools available to players. This is not the first time Zullie has done this: She has previously made videos zooming in on Elden Ring and Shadow of the Erdtree's NPCs . All the way back in 2016, she did the same for Dark Souls 3's cast .
Even with everything coming out right now, it's kind of a great time to revisit Elden Ring thanks to the Tarnished Edition. Even if you don't shell out for the new stuff, the servers will be more populated for the next few weeks than they likely ever will be again. And if you need help finding the new Tarnished Edition gear , PCG guides writer Sean Martin has got you covered.

title: The studio behind Star Wars Zero Company, which is currently a Steam bestseller, has reportedly furloughed the majority of its staff
text:
The studio behind Star Wars Zero Company furloughed up to 80 percent of its staff in the lead up to the RPG's launch, a Game File report reveals. That means affected staff are technically still employed by the company, but will receive no wage during the furlough period.
A representative from Bit Reactor confirmed the furloughs to Game File, though didn't indicate how many employees are affected. The rep said uncertainty around the game's launch performance was to blame for the furloughs, and that they were Bit Reactor's decision and not EA or Disney's.
Other sources claim up to 80% of the studio has been impacted. According to the Bit Reactor rep, it is hoped that furloughed workers will be brought back with full pay.
A former Bit Reactor staffer, Zachariah Scott, who was let go by the studio earlier this year, addressed the furloughs on LinkedIn yesterday. "It is sick and weird to have all of these EA and Disney folks as well as Bitreactor Senior staff making all of these 10/10 posts about Star Wars Zero Company being such a huge success and praising the work of the team while seemingly concealing the fact that the team was furloughed weeks ago," Scott wrote.
He went on: "It is a gross but all too common sight to see, another corporate game hitting the top of Steam while the team is left looking for work and cut off from any possible profit sharing. It would be such a different story if they had been upfront about it earlier, and now it feels like they're trying to keep the team in a holding pattern with good vibes and more empty promises."
Star Wars Zero Company was released on August 28 to near unanimous critical praise, with Ted Litchfield calling it "a new all-timer Star Wars game and a stunning debut for Bit Reactor". The tactical RPG is currently the top selling game on Steam right now, and that's only a third of the story: the game released for PS5 and Xbox consoles too.
It paints a pretty bleak picture of where the industry is at present: even a studio that has just shipped a critically acclaimed, well-selling Star Wars game published by EA is showing severe symptoms of decline in the days after launch.

title: MSI Crosshair 16 Max HX E2W review
text:
The MSI Crosshair 16 Max HX E2W is in many ways the polar opposite of the other MSI laptop I recently tested, the Stealth 16 AI+ B3W . The latter is an ultra-expensive, sleek and subtle machine that limits its power for the sake of thermals, efficiency, and form factor. Not so with the Crosshair: it's a gaming laptop, and it knows it.
I could tell as much as soon as I unboxed it, thanks to its glossy—and I would later discover, RGB-lit—embossed MSI logo on the lid, plus the general thickness, key styling and so on. It's not particularly obnoxious and still has some subtlety to it, but it's not hiding the fact that it's a gaming laptop.
Nor does it hide this fact when it comes to performance, eking as much as it can out of the RTX 5070 GPU and Core Ultra 7 251HX processor, saying to hell with thermals and battery life. I can certainly respect that, but it has to deliver in other respects, too, including price. And in other respects this laptop is not quite so pretty.
Buy if...
✅ You want great all-round performance: MSI really has designed this thing to eke out as much performance as possible from the mid-range components.
✅ Punchy visuals are important to you: This laptop has a gorgeous OLED panel that does indeed make visuals pop.
Do not buy if...
❌ You want snappy audio: The audio from this laptop suffers from latency issues, and I couldn't seem to resolve them even after quite a bit of tinkering.
❌ You want to take this out and about: Not only does this laptop have poor battery life, it also doesn't look particularly appealing aesthetically for use in public.

The particular Crosshair 16 Max HX E2W that I tested came with an Intel Core Ultra 7 251HX, RTX 5070, and 16 GB of DDR5 RAM, but there are different versions. The ones I can currently spot online have a more powerful Core Ultra 9 290HX with 32 GB of DDR5 , or the same 251HX CPU but an RTX 5060 and 32 GB of DDR5 . All of those come with 1 TB of storage.
In the case of the 16 GB of RAM in the version I have, it is at least 2x8 GB of fast 6,400 MT/s memory, rather than a single stick of slow RAM. This presumably helps a bunch with CPU-intensive tasks, as I found the laptop to perform even better than some others with 'better' CPUs.
A big draw here is also the OLED panel, which is gorgeous. I'm not used to seeing OLEDs on such gamer-y gaming laptops, as I've only really seen them on gaming laptops that are going for 'sleek and refined', so it's a nice surprise to see such a great panel here. It's only 165 Hz, but it's a perfect match for the RTX 5070 mobile GPU inside the Crosshair.
Future Future Future At first I thought there weren't many ports on this laptop, but before long I found the rest hidden on the rear side and breathed a sigh of relief. I particularly like the inclusion of a Thunderbolt 4 port as well as a port for an Ethernet connection.
Getting to how it is to actually use the laptop, I don't have any real complaints but equally no specific praises. It's no behemoth, but it's hardly a slimline laptop, either, and its keys feel simply… fine . WASD keys are translucent and there is 24-zone RGB, again signalling to the world 'I am definitely a gaming laptop'. I do wish MSI had foregone the numpad to make things a little less cramped, though. The trackpad is quite small, but it is at least central, which is the correct choice (fight me).
The big downside is audio, just as was the case with the Stealth. However, in this case it's even worse. There's definite (but not catastrophically high) latency over the default audio device, but unlike with the Stealth I tested, this wasn't resolved by switching to a different USB-connected audio device.
(Image credit: Future) As such, if you play games that really benefit from snappy and responsive audio such as shooters, and especially sensitive to a little audio delay, I'd steer clear unless and until MSI discovers what the problem is and how to fix it (the company is investigating). I tried disabling/uninstalling Nahimic as well as Norton antivirus to see if that helped, but doing the former proved difficult and the latter didn't resolve it.
The speakers themselves are nothing to write home about anyway. They're not the worst I've heard, but they've definitely got a little bit of that tinniness in them that you expect out of a lot of laptops or cheaper Bluetooth speakers.
MSI Crosshair 16 Max HX E2W performance
The Crosshair 16 Max HX E2W performs very well for an RTX 5070 laptop, often beating other similar lappies. MSI has clearly opted for a performance-oriented machine here, and it shows.

The MSI Crosshair 16 Max does run very hot on Extreme Performance mode (and, as an aside, still pretty damn hot in Balanced mode). That's especially the case for its Core Ultra 7 251HX CPU.
This laptop is indeed particularly toasty. This obviously helps in the performance department, but don't expect it to win any efficiency medals. 104 °C for the max CPU temp is hot , as is 84 °C for the GPU, though the new MSI Stealth runs a little hotter on that front.
That being said, during all my time gaming, I didn't notice my fingers getting too hot on WASD, and given the performance is so good, I doubt the high temps indicate too much throttling.
(Image credit: Future) The Crosshair can get pretty loud in Extreme Performance mode, which these benchmarks were taken in. However, as with the new Stealth, this Crosshair's fans don't sound grating at all. You just get a pleasant, loud whoosh. Though it will make it difficult to hear your game through the speakers if you're opting for built-in audio.
MSI Crosshair 16 Max HX E2W aesthetics
I don't have a ton of praise for the way this laptop looks, unfortunately. It's not awful, just not my particular cup of tea. There's a splash of the old-fashioned, angular, gamer-y look to it, but it only leans kind of half-heartedly in that direction, which ultimately means it looks a little confused about what it wants to be overall.
(Image credit: Future) You're getting some funky RGB lighting on the keys, including a translucent WASD if that's your jam, and you're also getting the logo on the lid which lights up and a particularly angular design on the underside, but the rest of the chassis is plain. To be honest, I'd rather it leaned in one direction or the other: gamer-y, or subtle. Still, it's far from an outrageous design and doesn't offend my aesthetic sensibilities too much.
MSI Crosshair 16 Max HX E2W software
The main bloatware on this laptop is Norton antivirus, which I'd personally promptly uninstall just because Microsoft Defender is fine and Norton, in my historical opinion, can be a bit of a pain.
(Image credit: MSI) Apart from that, you get MSI Center to control all the settings such as lighting and performance modes. You can install a bunch more modules to fiddle with different settings if you wish, but I just stuck with those and the default system info and options pages. It runs well and isn't too difficult to navigate once you get used to it, but it definitely feels like a 'set it and leave it' kind of software that you don't need to load up very often.

The MSI Crosshair 16 Max perhaps unsurprisingly doesn't do very well when it comes to battery life. It seems oriented around eking out as much performance as possible from its CPU and GPU, without much care for efficiency.
You probably already expected this given the laptop ekes out as much performance as it can from its components, not to mention that it runs mighty hot, but battery life is not great. This isn't a laptop for those of you who primarily want to game while out and about using battery power, but for short sessions or light work it's fine unplugged.
The RTX 5080-boasting MSI Stealth laptop I tested has a 90 Wh battery and lasted for 104 minutes in a gaming battery life benchmark, whereas this one has an 80 Wh battery and lasted for just 72 minutes. That's 31% less time up and running, and less than a bunch of other RTX 5070 laptops we've tested.
MSI Crosshair 16 Max HX E2W Value
You're looking at about $2,600 for the 32 GB version of this— $2,000 on offer —and I can't see the 16 GB version that I tried for sale anywhere. Looking at some of the best deals on gaming laptops right now, that $2,600 is pretty expensive for an RTX 5070 machine.
On the one hand, this isn't a corner-cutting machine, as you're getting a lovely OLED panel and some very convincing performance that pushes the CPU and GPU as far as possible. But on the other hand, even $2,000 on sale is a lot for an RTX 5070 machine, even during a memory shortage. You can often pick similar but non-OLED gaming laptops up for well under $1,500 on sale.
Future Future Future Future As such, unless and until there are bigger discounts on it, I don't think the price tag fits what's on offer. If the normal retail price were a couple hundred lower and the discount price was a couple hundred lower, too, I would consider it for the OLED panel and great performance.
But as it stands, it's a tough sell, especially if you want any kind of battery or thermal efficiency, or just a laptop that looks a little more dashing. Not to mention one that doesn't suffer from audio latency issues. Considering performance alone it's a great machine, but the price is not quite right.

title: Nekome: Nazi Hunter is about gleefully butchering fascists in Germany and America, but its devs swear it's not political
text:
A thing that often happens in this line of work is: a developer or PR person enthusiastically trying to convince you that a not-especially-interesting game is actually incredibly innovative and exciting. The Gamescom demo for Nekome: Nazi Hunter is the first time I have been in the reverse position: I thought the game was interesting, well-timed, and politically bold—the studio was keen to convince me it wasn't.
The demo of Nekome I played goes hard. The Nazi haut-monde—an identikit line-up of chisel-jawed pigs—has gathered for a sumptuous dinner, and to chortle with one another about European death camps and the inevitable victory of the Aryan race over its lessers. Only one figure stands out: the meek waiter, with dark hair and skin, who caps off the boss Nazi's opening speech by revealing a severed Wehrmacht head beneath a silver cloche.
Under your control, he proceeds to stab every unarmed Nazi in the room to death.
The devs at ProbablyMonsters told me afterwards that they were not "political" and that Nekome was not making a political statement. Well, they had me fooled.
But let's get mechanical. I suspect a lot of people will, justifiably, find the deficiencies of Nekome's movement and combat too much to bear. In the demo I played, it all just felt a little off—animations did not blend together nicely, the camera would get hung up on objects and enemies, and the actual process of beating a fascist to death erupted in clunky staccato movements rather than the fluid, dancelike combat of Arkham. It's by no means dreadful, but it doesn't feel great to play.
(Image credit: ProbablyMonsters) But man , it has style. It's pure grindhouse, and the safe-to-discuss, entirely non-political influences ProbablyMonsters was happy to speak to me about—like Tarantino's Inglourious Basterds—are on happy display. Every fascist is a fountain of gore waiting to happen; once you beat them to within an inch of their life, you can unleash finishers whereby Vano—the game's young Romani protagonist whose entire family was murdered in front of him in an act of senseless Nazi violence—will use a knife to unzip his enemies in dramatic fashion.
Kill enough Nazis, and you can dip into a focus mode, whereby you can select distinct Nazi body parts on which to vent your righteous fury. Once your foes are dead, you will find yourself constantly confronted with prompts to "desecrate corpse" as you stumble over their remains during combat. Take the game's advice, and Vano will do a little extra violence. As a treat.
(Image credit: ProbablyMonsters) All of this is punctuated by cinematic touches. Frame lines on Nekome's 'film reel' will become visible as Vano's violence reaches more absurd heights, as if the game simply can't contain his rage.
All very fun and gleefully OTT, yes, but the bit where Nekome really got me leaning forward—where I became convinced this might be a game that had something to say, was when it transplanted the action from Europe over to the US of A. It's not just SS men Vano cuts up, he also takes on the German American Bund: the real-life pro-Nazi organisation that attempted to work its tendrils into the USA in the years leading up to the Second World War.
(Image credit: ProbablyMonsters) American fascists attack Vano's WW1-vet mentor, so off he goes to their offices to do what he does best, muttering that "These Americans have sworn themselves to a morally bankrupt cause," as he smashes up their printing presses and beats them to death with fists, bottles, and, at one point, a free-standing ashtray.
It's stylish, fun, janky and, during a time of worldwide far-right revival, deeply cathartic. I found myself bemused to be told by Nekome's makers that their game about slaughtering hordes of European and American Nazis—at a time when European and American Nazis are a lot more prominent in real life than they have been for a while—had no explicit politics whatsoever.
(Image credit: ProbablyMonsters) They did tell me one thing, though, when I asked if Vano's bloody quest for vengeance would leave me filled with regret by the game's end: "I don't think you'll feel bad about killing Nazis in this game." Well, that'll have to do.

title: Fable system requirements seem reasonable but with a 30 fps target and no mention of upscaling it's hard to say for sure
text:
With Fable (it's just called Fable, but it's technically Fable 4) set to release on February 23 next year, we finally have its system requirements. And for a big budget game launching in 2027, they're not too bad.
That's according to the newly updated Fable FAQ , which says you will need an Intel i7 6850K or an AMD Ryzen 5 2600, paired with either an RTX 5050 / RTX 2060 , a Radeon RX 6600 , or an Intel A580 to run the game on a minimum. Minimum in this case means running the game at 1080p at 30 fps.
With the RTX 2060 being a budget-to-mid-range graphics card from 2019, and both suggested CPUs being nearly a decade old, these are reasonably unintensive requirements, assuming you can stomach 30 fps. Especially for what looks to be a very good-looking game .
The recommended specs ( which in this case means running the game on Medium ) are an Intel i5 11600KF or AMD Ryzen 5 5600 paired with an RTX 5060 / RTX 3060 TI , or an AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT / RX 7600 XT . There's no Intel GPU mention on this one, and 'recommended' entails playing the game on 1440p at 30 fps or at 1200p at 60 fps.

Interestingly, there is no note on whether upscaling is used to get these figures. Forza Horizon 6 , another game from the Fable developer, Playground Games, specifies that its system requirements do not include upscaling (apart from the Extreme RT recommendation), so the lack of any such declaration is certainly rather strange.
And upscaling has been finding its way into system requirements recently. For instance, The Blood of Dawnwalker's final system requirements included upscaling set to Balanced, which made them appear lower than previously given system requirements.
With the game still a good few months out, these may not be the absolute final requirements, but they paint a good picture of what you could roughly expect out of your rig.
Still, early signs are decent here, and the 12 GB memory requirement isn't too bad, even with the memory crisis in full swing. In fact, with the memory crisis also taking the price of SSDs with it, its 135 GB of storage requirement may be the hardest for me to make room for. Hey, maybe you've got a few hundred GB in your recycle bin like I did a buddy of mine had.

title: Dwarf Fortress creator says the industry's in shambles over AI and layoff-happy CEOs: 'Everyone I know, their bosses are slowly getting psychosis'
text:
The game industry is—to use the lightest possible language—in an interesting spot. While videogames are as profitable as ever on paper , we've had a few consecutive years of brutal layoffs and studio closures , as well as all of the knock-on impacts that the advent of generative AI (and the subsequent and boneheaded insistence that it's the future) has had. Billions in spending , skyrocketing hardware prices, the whole kit and caboodle.
Which, once more , has exhausted Dwarf Fortress' creator Tarn Adams, who spoke to PC Gamer's Joshua Wolens during Gamescom 2026 : "They're trying to have a CEO press a button that makes a game, and then everyone else somehow buys it without a job. So I don't see that going anywhere sustainable, and I feel like there will simply be a pop and a reckoning and then [it's on repeat] unless people do something else."
Adams says it's not just games that've been suffering, either: "I mean, everyone I know, their bosses are slowly getting psychosis, right? They're just like, 'Yeah, but did you use AI on your commits?' And they're like, 'Oh well, I'm not happy with this guy,' you know. 'We'll probably have machines do the job'.
"It just reminds me of like a fucking Dead Kennedys song or something. It's just the same old shit. I mean, they laid off my dad from the sewage treatment plant because they didn't understand what his job was, and he was the computer guy there, and then they don't have a company anymore, so it's like it's the same shit."
He's not exactly wrong—it's not as if the current industry problems are unprecedented, or came out of nowhere. Since the advent of modern capitalism (and likely a long while before that), those in charge have often misunderstood, underestimated, or dismissed the hard work that goes into labour they don't understand.
It's become particularly nasty with generative AI, however, because now said CEOs can still see an end result that mimics the thing they don't understand—and are able to self-delude themselves into thinking it's replicable at scale, or that it's even producing the same quality as the product they've actually been selling.
After all, if actual studies are being done into AI-induced psychosis that's impacting us serfs, there's nothing to say the executive suite is immune, either. Especially given that a lot of them don't even understand why others are put off.
"It's been going on forever. That was before AI—or this form of AI," Adams says, before lamenting: "They took the letters from me! I have to talk about dwarf behavior now. I can't even talk about dwarf AI. It doesn't exist. It's dwarf behavior , and they misbehave sometimes."

title: Persona 4 Revival won't finally realize Yosuke's gay romance because Atlus thinks it'd have to let you kiss every other guy, too
text:
With Persona 4 Revival giving my favourite game a modern-day makeover, I was hoping Atlus would use it as an opportunity to reintroduce features that didn't make the cut the first time around. You know, like a certain romance between protagonist Yu Narukami and his bestie Yosuke Hanamura.
Both English and Japanese voiced dialogue was found in the original game which heavily implied a planned romance between the two, though it never made an appearance in either Persona 4 or Persona 4 Golden. Revival's announcement had fans buzzing in anticipation of its addition, but unfortunately that isn't happening.
(Image credit: Atlus) I had the opportunity to sit down with producer Kazuhisa Wada and art director Akane Kabayashi at Gamescom 2026, where the former told me that Yosuke will once again remain in the friendzone for Persona 4 Revival. "We heard rumours of all the people wanting the Yosuke romance, and we were thinking about doing it.
"But then we were like, if we do Yosuke we kind of have to do it for all the guys. And if we did all the guys, that would be so much additional content that would be a lot of work. We gotta keep things fair, right? So we ended up being like 'Ah, this might be a little bit much, so I think we're gonna have to pass.'"
I think I might actually have to disagree with Wada here. While I think it would be cool to see a full protagsexual ensemble, I also would have really liked to see Yosuke's previously cut romance implemented in a meaningful way. It also does a lot of legwork in reframing who Yosuke is and why he behaves the way he does—he frequently makes homophobic remarks in the original Persona 4, but redefining it from the perspective of someone who also has feelings for the protagonist adds a helluva lot of depth to his character.
Of course, I do expect Atlus to be pruning and tweaking some of Yosuke's more out-of-pocket dialogue in Revival, though I think it would've better served his character to retain it with the additional framing of his queerness.
Though if Atlus had made every man romanceable in the game, would that have included Teddie? Well, as Kabayashi put it: "Does Teddie count as the guy? Yes, of course he does." Look at what we've lost.

title: Linux manages to avoid the age verification apocalypse, but SteamOS isn't in the clear yet
text:
California's Digital Age Assurance Act is due to take effect at the very start of 2027 , bringing in sweeping age-verification checks by system providers. As part of it, operating systems will have to do age checks on users to lock down certain functions, which had led some Linux developers to go full crisis mode in response. Well, good news, the Assembly Bill 1856 amendment has just passed and it exempts open-source operating systems from compliance.
As reported by Tom's Hardware , the amendment passed with a 39-0 vote. The wording on the Linux passage is curious. It specifically precludes a "person or entity that distributes an operating system or application under license terms that permit a recipient to copy, redistribute, and modify the software" from being called an "operating system provider." That means Linux users will get away without verifying age on somewhat of a definitional technicality.
The amendment also ensures that operating system providers acquire "only the minimum amount of information necessary to comply" with the age check, and therefore this should stop providers from acquiring more information on users, or even spying on users for their own benefit, any more than necessary through the guise of Californian law.
Though Linux and its many distros will be exempt from the law, it's not too clear yet if Valve's SteamOS is. SteamOS is a Linux-based OS built on Arch, but it also has proprietary elements, which means one can't copy, redistribute, and modify it. Even if SteamOS is exempt, you will still have to verify your age via Steam on your Steam Machine or Steam Deck if you want to play certain games.
Affected operating systems included Windows, Android, macOS, and iOS. The bill was originally introduced back in February and at that time was deemed to include Linux , but it looks like the authorities saw sense before it passed. Ensuring these checks could've been immensely damaging to the use of open source operating systems in the state, not the least bit Silicon Valley.
The last few years have seen all manner of age checks roll out. Discord preemptively agreed to age verification checks , but clarified many wouldn't have to, as it already has the information necessary to verify ages . That's somewhat worrying, but it does mean not having to give your ID or face to the company.
And with Discord's rollout having ties to Palantir, and no one particularly liking the idea of giving their information to the government, there's already quite a lot of cynicism around digital age checks. Earlier this year, the UK's Online Safety Act came into full force , even requiring me to verify my age on my phone to get full access.
Linux's user base has been growing off the back of Microsoft's many failures , and getting around age verification checks is just one more step for the OS. It seems 2026 may have finally been the year of the Linux, but who said it can't have two years in a row?

title: Nvidia snuck me into a room to show off DLSS 5 in person, and it's somehow beautiful, ugly, impressive, and troubling all at the same time
text:
I think it's fair to say that DLSS 5 is the most controversial Nvidia creation… well, ever. After the huge amounts of backlash it received in reaction to its unveiling earlier this year , Nvidia's AI image enhancing tech has been mostly kept under lock and key.
However, myself and a select group of journalists were ushered into a small room in the Nvidia booth at Gamescom last week, amid some furtive glances and hushed whispering. As the lights went down, it became obvious as to why. Here was the latest version of DLSS 5 running in front of us, the controversial graphics tech in the flesh. And the message Nvidia wanted to get across was deliberate, and strongly put: It's all about developer control.
I was shown a character sitting within the Nvidia Zorah demo, the same shown at SIGGRAPH 2026 earlier this year. As he sat, looking around at his environment in a bored fashion, I leaned forward in my chair. DLSS 5 was obviously altering the image to a significant degree, but seeing the results in person, it was clear this was nowhere near the " yassified Grace " level of AI enhancement shown in the first reveal.
Our digital example, casually inspecting the back of his hand, looked a lot like the original character model—but with more photorealistic lighting, and plenty of finer details that seemed fitting for the scene. It was nowhere near as brash an image as I was expecting, I'll say that much for free.
At the side of the screen was the DLSS 5 developer control menu. Two sliders, marked "structure intensity" and "tone intensity" were set somewhere around the midway mark—and at these settings, the character looked pretty damn good.
Nvidia Nvidia There are more tools for developers to play with, too. The masking feature allows devs to select individual items in a scene (say, a fruit bowl on a table) and give it the AI-enhanced treatment, while leaving everything else DLSS 5-free. The varying AI models can also be switched in and out (or on and off) on a whim.
According to Nvidia, the fine-tuning abilities of DLSS 5 are designed to be as developer-friendly as possible, allowing them to dip in and out of its features on a model-per-model basis to suit their artistic intent. Seeing the demo running in front of me with my own eyes, I could feel myself coming around to the idea. My arms uncrossed.
Nvidia Nvidia Nvidia And then my hosts began messing with the sliders and the model presets, and an essential truth emerged. While a light dusting of DLSS 5 can cause a substantial visual leap in terms of photorealism, turning it up to 11 can still provoke an unwanted, gut-level reaction.
Turning DLSS 5 up to 11 can still provoke an unwanted, gut-level reaction
There are three image-transforming AI models for devs to choose from (at least in the demo I was shown): A, B, and C. While models A and C looked pretty good to me at various settings, model B made me wince when both sliders were pushed up. The HDR-like shadows became overblown, the skin textures too shiny, the facial features too keenly drawn.
To my eyes, characters with model B turned up can look substantially different from the model underneath, in a way that's reminiscent of the AI beauty filters we've all become far too familiar with. In short, it's still capable of giving me the ick.
Nvidia Nvidia I'll call it as I see it: DLSS 5 turned up to the guns, particularly using model B, can look downright ugly. But Nvidia's point makes a whole lot of sense. It's the developers, the artists behind the game, that choose how far to push the technology. If it oversteps the mark? Devs can adjust the settings and rein it back in, and you can turn it off entirely (separate from regular DLSS upscaling) if you disagree with their choices.
On that note, some Nvidia staff members I spoke to took issue with the idea that DLSS 5, even in the experimental version shown earlier this year, is capable of transforming the facial geometry of a character model. I argued the contrary, because well, look at the screenshots below.
Nvidia Nvidia Apparently, this is more of a perceived effect created by the lighting than an actual, DLSS 5-induced facelift. This eventually turned into a philosophical debate, where I argued that, even if it simply looks like the model is creating markedly different facial geometry from the original character models, the end result is functionally the same.
Because that's what it looks like, and what it looks like is the whole point. This argument resulted in a stalemate, so I'll let you be the judge for yourselves.
Anyway, the longer the demos continued, the clearer it became that DLSS 5 is capable of creating some stunning imagery when handled with a delicate touch, and some seriously overblown results when pushed to the limit. DLSS 5 can enhance—but it can also alter an image with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer.
(Image credit: Nvidia) The example above shows a DLSS 5-enhanced scene of some foliage against a building, with ray tracing turned on and off. It's supposed to demonstrate that the more lighting information you give the models to work with, the better the visual result. The DLSS 5 and ray-traced image combined, though, looks seriously oversaturated to my eyes. Realism has gone out of the window, and the end result is… lurid, to say the least.
What is beautiful to some is garish to others, but all I'll say is that the term "better" is far from my mind. There's no accounting for taste, is there?
(Image credit: Nvidia) What we're going to be relying on for the most part, though, are the tastes of the game developers themselves. I was taken into a separate room to try out NBA 2K27, the first game you'll be able to play with DLSS 5 enabled. Officially, at least , as it can apparently be modded into any game.
This was a very locked down session, in which the devs refused to be drawn in on the details of exactly what sort of DLSS 5 implementation I was looking at. However, I'd guess that, by Nvidia's standards, everything I saw was achieved by using the lower end of the DLSS 5 spectrum.
If developers tune it wisely, there are real visual benefits to be seen
The sweat running down the players' arms looked… sweatier. More glistening. The facial features looked more realistic, with better lighting in the nooks and crannies of their various mugs, and less of the "uncanny valley" effect I'd seen at higher settings. The crowd in the background transformed from low-poly models into a more passable depiction of basketball match attendees, without straying too far from the look of the original assets.
Nvidia Nvidia Nvidia Nvidia To my surprise, I didn't experience the AI image ick. It looked more like the difference between a game running on a console, and one running on PC with a ton of extra graphics options added on top. DLSS 5 doesn't look quite so revolutionary at these settings, perhaps—but the results impressed me more than I expected.
I was careful to look for signs of ghosting, or any morphing AI faces under fast motion. One of my critiques of the previous DLSS 5 footage was the temporal handling, which looked a little blurred and smeared to my eyes. However, there was no hint of that here. I played virtual basketball, I sucked at it, and I enjoyed the look of the game overall.
In all honesty, it felt like playing a next-gen game with cutting-edge graphics technology, and not an ill-advised AI gaming revolution. This, beyond anything else, was perhaps the best demonstration that DLSS 5 can be used to genuinely enhance the look of our games, rather than turning them into an AI-slathered mess. If developers tune it wisely, there are real visual benefits to be seen.
Nvidia Nvidia All of this might be a moot point, though, if performance is a concern. The Nvidia devs I spoke to estimated a 50-60% performance hit with DLSS 5 turned on, which doesn't vary on a game-by-game basis. Essentially, it's still a massive resource hog as things stand, although it no longer requires two RTX 5090s just to run. Goodie.
Further performance improvements are forthcoming, says Nvidia, but my eyebrows jumped so high at this news I'm surprised they didn't shoot off the top of my head. Graphics card prices are outrageous right now , and I can't help wondering who's going to want to slice their frame rate in half in return for some AI-enhanced imagery, good-looking or otherwise.
Nvidia Nvidia Nvidia All of the performance charts I was shown used a combination of 6x Multi Frame Generation and various levels of upscaling to bump up the numbers. And while I'm not as much of a frame generation sceptic as some, I doubt this will come as good news to those curious to try out the tech.
If the performance impact was minimal, I could see some gamers experimenting with DLSS 5 for themselves and potentially changing their minds. With this sort of massive dip, though, I think DLSS 5's GPU-hogging ways are a much bigger issue for adoption than the AI-ified nature of the tech itself.
(Image credit: Nvidia) What's left, then, is the thorny issue of the ethical debate. The elephant in the room, and there's no getting around it, is that generative AI usage in games is a massive hot topic at the moment. In fact, AI usage in general is causing all sorts of debates in all sorts of arenas, from the potential effects on the job market , to ecological concerns , to discussions around the very nature of truth .
We're going to have to decide for ourselves if we want to engage with it
And this, I feel, is the real hurdle Nvidia is trying to jump. While it's clear that DLSS 5 can be beneficial to the image quality of our games in the right hands, whether we, as gamers, want to participate in the AI-ification of everything in this way is much more doubtful. And it's on this level where I feel far more conflicted about the tech.
My criticisms of the AI revolution, in a general sense, are well documented . And while I can absolutely see the potential benefits of DLSS 5, I left the demo booth with mixed feelings. Is this where the games industry is heading? Will I be spending most of my gaming time looking at more AI-enhanced imagery in the future?
(Image credit: Nvidia) Will developers make use of the tech wisely, or will major releases eventually go for the full yassified approach, transforming our games into something unrecognisable from what they are today? Will devs jump in with both feet, or will they be more cautious ? And crucially, is AI-enhanced imagery really what we want, even if it's capable of looking nice?
In principle, the demos I was shown should have me jumping up and down with excitement at the potential of better gaming graphics. But the AI association, perhaps even infiltration, into a form of media I truly adore is enough to keep me awake at night. In practice, DLSS 5 is certainly capable of creating some good-looking imagery in the right hands.
But it also represents a major leap towards an AI-enhanced gaming future, and one that still makes me, in the depths of my bones, more than a little uncomfortable. Whatever the case, DLSS 5 will be launching on September 3—and we're going to have to decide for ourselves if we want to engage with it.

title: DLSS 5 comes with a massive 50-60% performance hit, so I hope you like lower frame rates with your dose of AI image enhancement
text:
I walked into Nvidia's DLSS 5 demo last week with some preconceptions, I'll be honest. I hadn't enjoyed the images it had produced to date, and I was sceptical about the benefits it could bring to our beloved games. Not to mention the troubling notion of AI-altered images entering into our hobby, even if you can turn them off with a simple checkbox.
The good news is, DLSS 5 is capable of looking pretty good once the settings have been tweaked by actual game developers. The very bad news is, Nvidia says turning DLSS 5 on will currently reduce performance by 50-60%. And that's across the board—no matter the game.
Nvidia was keen to point out that, just six months ago, DLSS 5 required two RTX 5090s to run . So, a 5x improvement since then is something to hold within our collective hats. But tanking frame rates is very unlikely to improve DLSS 5's perception within the PC gaming community, that's for certain.
Looking at the basic performance charts Nvidia has provided us so far, the ultra-high frame rate figures are based on 6x Multi Frame Generation . So, while the little RTX 5060 can churn out a 258 fps result in NBA 2K27 at 1080p Ultra settings with ray tracing and DLSS 5 enabled, the game underneath will actually be running at around 43 fps.
At 4K, the same game settings result in a 370 fps average on an RTX 5090 , or a 233 fps average on an RTX 5080 . That's with Performance-level upscaling, though, and with 6x MFG doing some seriously heavy lifting once more.
Nvidia Nvidia Nvidia If you've spent thousands of bucks on a high-end graphics card, I'd imagine that running games with the upscaling and frame generation settings near their limits to achieve high frame rates is probably not what you had in mind.
All of which makes me wonder if the AI-ification of DLSS 5 is really the biggest barrier to its acceptance. I have my own deep, dark concerns about DLSS 5, AI in general, and its hooks making their way into our hobby. But if the tech is capable of slicing the frame rate in half, all of this might be a moot point.
The Nvidia folk I spoke to were keen to point out that performance improvements are already on the way. But given that so many gamers are stuck with older graphics cards, thanks to the ongoing pricing crisis that seems destined to become much worse before it gets better, I do wonder who the tech is currently for.
(Image credit: Nvidia) When ray tracing first arrived on the scene , its performance-tanking qualities were at least (partially) offset by the introduction of upscaling. But all these years later, I still debate for myself whether it's worth turning on when I play games on my own, relatively high-end gaming PC. Our rigs might be better equipped on average, but ray tracing is still a performance hog in 2026—and many gamers I speak to still turn it off for smoother frames.
And while DLSS 5 is certainly more... transformative than ray tracing in terms of the images it creates, it's also far more controversial. Even if you're prepared to make the jump into AI-enhanced games (and it's quite the leap, let's be honest), putting those concerns in tandem with massively compromised frame rates is a seriously big ask for even the most curious of gamers.
I expected to be writing about the controversy surrounding Nvidia's new tech in terms of the wider atmosphere of AI discontent . But here I am getting down to brass tacks. In its current form, DLSS 5 seems to hit your graphics card like a freight train—and whatever your opinion on AI in gaming, nobody wants that.

title: The Witcher 3 Remastered should run just fine on the Steam Deck, say devs
text:
As is the case with a lot of older games (I regret to inform you that The Witcher 3 is 11 years old) that get the remaster treatment, there's been some anxiety over whether The Witcher 3 Remastered will run properly on the Steam Deck—especially given it'll be a free update . It's always frustrating when some new glossy graphics pack messes with your hardware.
Well, fear not—speaking to PC Gamer's Joshua Wolens ahead of Gamescom 2026 , CD Projekt Red's executive producer of external projects Jakub Kutrzuba has told us that The Witcher 3 Remastered will run just as well on your Steam Deck, thanks to general optimisation improvements with the new rendering engine.
"When it comes to Steam Deck, based on what we see, the game will work the same way, but look much much better. Because from one side we are bringing all these improvements, we are bringing new content, we are upgrading the assets, but [we also have] the new rendering features."
These features, Kutrzuba says, give the game more hardware budget for all those fancy spangled new assets and textures: "With the newer rendering engine, many of the systems just work faster. So we are just capable of showing a more beautiful image with the same cost, and this is also the case for the Nintendo Switch 2, which is coming together with the Remaster as well."
So, no, the Remaster isn't some monster that'll eat all of your Steam Deck's RAM. In general, CD Projekt seems to've learned its lesson after the horror show of Cyberpunk 2077, with its developers boasting solid performance out of The Witcher 4 , as well. You'll be able to engage in some cosy, lo-fi monster slaying in the windswept, freshly-beautified White Orchard without fretting about frame drops.
Which is good, because given Wolens' stellar impression of the Remaster's graphical update , you'll want to.

title: I've spent four months testing control pads in Counter-Strike and I've finally settled on my fave
text:
Most gamers enjoy a speedy or balanced feel to their mouse pad, but there are a few of us out there who have a penchant for stopping power. If you're into tactical shooters that require very steady aim plus occasional flicks with a precise stop on your enemy's head, slower control pads are for you.
I've been trying out some different control pads in Counter-Strike 2 for months now and I feel like I'm finally able to draw some solid conclusions over which are best. At least as far as my own fingertips are concerned. Your mileage may of course vary.
Personal favourite: Zowie H-SR III
Noteworthy: Wallhack CR-005
Key terms
Stopping power: How easy it is to stop your mouse where and when you want it to, presumably over an enemy's head.
Static friction: How hard it is to get the mouse moving from stationary. The combination of this and dynamic friction makes for good stopping power.
Dynamic friction: How hard it is to keep the mouse moving when in motion. The combination of this and static friction makes for good stopping power.
Softer pads: Tend to be slower.
Harder pads: Tend to be faster.

Razer's Gigantus V2 Pro is great if you really have a thing for slow pads and don't much care what you have to sacrifice to get it. The surface, which Razer says was made to match the pro player's NiKo 's preference, is indeed very slow—slower than any I've used. This means little chance of accidentally nudging your crosshair out of line when holding an angle.
However, it's a bit too slow for my liking, and I'm saying this as someone who massively prefers control pads to speed ones now for playing CS2. I think the slowness is in part thanks to how soft the pad is as it's noticeably softer than any other I've tried.
But if something super-slow is your thing—and who can argue with one of the best Counter-Strike players of all time?—it'll serve you well. Also note there's even a Max Control version that is, presumably, even slower than this one.

It's smaller than the others and is a little too quick for my liking in a control pad, feeling a bit closer to a regular cloth pad than I'd like. In particular, I notice that with this pad I have to try a little harder to keep my crosshair steady when holding a headshot angle.
Still, it does look nice and it is slower and more controlled than many other (non-control) options on the market—it's certainly slower than speed pads. If you prefer a little more speed to your control and don't mind your competitive pad being a bit on the smaller side, the MM Pro is a reasonable choice.

I was immediately sold on this Zowie pad when I tried it. It ticks every box for me and is what I keep returning to as my baseline for playing Counter-Strike. That's because it manages to maintain a level of static friction that keeps my crosshair steady when holding angles, but is just on that cusp where I can also move my mouse pretty easily for flicks.
There's also its dynamic friction, ie, how it feels when actually moving the mouse. On this front, the H-SR III doesn't just have a decent amount of slowness/muddiness to it but also a texture that you can subtly feel as you move. It might be the placebo effect, but I feel like that's helped my muscle memory a little when aiming in-game.
Then there's the fact that it's a pretty hard pad for cloth, which means you don't get much inconsistency to how much your mouse drags depending on how hard you press. That can make all the difference in clutch moments when you tense up and push down harder. I really don't have anything to complain about here, which is why the Zowie is my go-to. Instead of opting for a slow cloth, SteelSeries has given this pad quite a smooth and hard-topped but very rough texture. You can really feel your mouse moving across it, which does help your muscle memory. Stopping power is pretty good, too.
On the other hand, static friction isn't quite as good as on the Zowie pad, and dynamic friction might be a touch quicker, too, though it's hard to tell. Most importantly, though, the rough texture can be quite unpleasant on your arm when gaming for an extended period if you're a low-sens player as many control pad gamers are. However, it still doesn't quite match a good cloth control pad for, well, control. After breaking it in a little, I found it to be more speedy than the Zowie and even the Corsair. It's still not as fast as speed pads though, and the static friction is particularly nice for a glass pad.
The main benefit of going glass is that it should last a very long time, unlike a cloth pad which wears out pretty quickly. It will also have consistent friction and glide however hard you press into it. The downsides are not being able to roll it up, potentially having to wear a gaming sleeve to prevent your arm sticking , having to replace your mouse skates more often as they get worn down, and having to wipe it down pretty frequently to keep dust away.
If it was a little slower and more controlled I think I'd make these sacrifices for the consistency and longevity of a glass pad, but it's just not quite there yet for control players compared to cloth. Saying that, even if it's not quite as slow as some cloth options, it's impressive that Wallhack has managed to make a glass pad as slow as this. It means glass pad lovers who play tac FPS need to miss out no longer.

title: Afterworld, Paradox's post-apocalyptic grand strategy game, let me conquer Florida with a band of alcoholic mutant cannibals
text:
With Afterworld , Paradox Development Studio is giving the post-apocalypse the Stellaris treatment, turning the end times into a ludicrously elaborate sandbox where you can live out all sorts of apocalyptic fantasies—whether you want to create a freewheeling band of road warriors or a new American empire.
I went to Sweden to play an alpha build of this ambitious behemoth last month, and I've been able to keep playing at home since then. But this is a Paradox game, so I still feel like I'm barely scraping its dusty, radioactive surface.
Here's a bit of what I've been getting up to, across multiple playthroughs:
I made a band of alcoholic mutant cannibals, stole some bikes, and conquered Florida.
I embraced the religion of the highway, creating a tribe of zealous petrol heads spreading their beliefs across the wasteland.
I teamed up with an ancient immortal to help rebuild America, betrayed him, and tore the continent apart with our brutal civil war.
I created a docile empire of slaves by making everyone addicted to drugs.
I became a cheese magnate.
Even in this alpha build, with its single origin and only one major threat, there's plenty to do—enough to give this would-be conqueror a bit of a headache, frankly. OK, before I get too far ahead of myself, here's the setup.
Leaving the vault
(Image credit: Paradox) You are a band of survivors in the North American wasteland. Like Stellaris, you'll have a variety of starting options—your band's origins—but in this build there's only the Shelterborn. Think Fallout's vault dwellers. This gives you a bespoke starting scenario, where your vault is about to go kaboom and you've got to find a new place to live on the surface.
Unlike Stellaris, however, these origins let you give some input. In the Shelterborn origin, for instance, you get to decide how your survivors handled food riots, and if they want to rebuild America or dominate what remains. Your choices determine the character of your band and their starting resources.
Unlike Stellaris, however, these origins let you give some input.
From there you'll build and upgrade settlements, join up with other bands, explore ruins, create laws and belief systems, and butt heads with powerful dominions—sprawling empires ruled by immortals who were born before the collapse of civilisation. Dominions are a bit like Stellaris's fallen and awakened empires, in that they are established and immensely powerful right at the start of the game.
Afterworld's alpha purposefully puts you right in the path of its sole dominion, ruled by Citizen Farouk. He's just a responsible patriot who wants to rebuild America. He's even going to hold an election to pick the 'president of presidents'. Sure, he's going to make sure it's him, but you can trust him. Definitely. 100%.
(Image credit: Paradox) Refusing to join Farouk always leads to war. At first he just sends other bands who have joined him to do his dirty work, but eventually he gets sick of the disrespect and sends in the big guns. Huge, mechanised armies that you'll have no hope of fighting off until the endgame. Joining him doesn't mean you'll have to be loyal, though.
I refused to pay his tithes, rejected all of his requests, and slowly built up my own power base. It wasn't until I became pretty powerful myself and stood against him in the election that Farouk truly woke up, kicking off an apocalyptic civil war that I've so far not been able to win. This isn't just because Farouk's armies are massive and much better equipped—it's also because I really hate fighting wars in Afterworld.
The UI and map just aren't up to the challenge of making these big fights easy to parse yet, and the Whac-A-Mole problem that appears in a lot of Paradox games is so much more pronounced here. War just feels too much like a grind. That said, most conflicts I became embroiled in ended swiftly. It's incredibly easy to just steamroll foes if you've got some bikes and guns.
Fighting is further complicated by Afterworld's multitude of manufacturing and supply chains. It's an evolution of the Hearts of Iron 4 model and is actually the one part of Afterworld's warfare that I like. Every single weapon and vehicle that you use must be either built or found, and then you also need to keep manufacturing fuel and bullets, which require both resources and buildings.
End times economics
(Image credit: Paradox) In this way, Afterworld evokes logistics-heavy city builders and survival games, and it makes creating and maintaining a well-armed force feel like a real achievement—one that you're rewarded for, as all this equipment will make it incredibly easy for you to expand if you have conquest in mind.
Even if you're not set on a path of domination, however, the resource economy will still be central to all of your playthroughs. Resource scarcity is one of the main drivers behind exploration and conflict, and so many of the decisions I made came down to a need for more fuel or batteries or simply food and water.
But this isn't a survival game, and Paradox has been a bit more generous due to this fact. If you don't have enough food or water, it isn't the end for your tribe. It just stunts population growth and harms the health of each individual band in your tribe, which makes them more dissatisfied with the way things are being run.
Finding the resources you need, either through theft or exploration or settling a region that naturally produces them, is only half of the puzzle. You'll need other resources to build ways to extract those resources or manufacture them into something more useful, and then you need to consider what bands are running the show.
(Image credit: Paradox) While you start off with a single band, you'll end up juggling a lot more of them in your tribe, and every single one of them is treated as a separate entity with their own characters, beliefs and skills. You can choose where they sit in the tribe's hierarchy, and give them territory to govern. If you've got a band with a green thumb, then, you'll want to put them in charge of your tribe's bread basket.
Once a band is under your control, you are in charge of its progression, and I found myself compelled to create a list of things I needed and then pick bands to take care of those things, always choosing the option that enhanced their ability to do so whenever they levelled up.
You can finish a game in a weekend.
It's a level of population management that I haven't encountered in other Paradox games before, and I appreciate the level of fine control it offers. It also works well for this zoomed in setting. You're not trying to conquer the world or a galaxy—you've just got North America to worry about. So this granularity feels manageable.
Another significant difference compared to most of Paradox's games is Afterworld's pace. You can finish a game in a weekend. Within a couple of hours, you can go from being a one-band tribe scrounging around for food and water to a burgeoning empire. And the randomness of exploration means that your tribe's warriors could be decked out in plasma guns and accompanied by mechs while you're still figuring out the game's basics.
Snowballing
(Image credit: Paradox) You can definitely become too strong too quickly, so there's some balancing required, but I hope Paradox maintains some of the random leaps in power. It feels true to the post-apocalyptic genre. A band of nobodies discovering some pre-fall tech that catapults them into the limelight is a fun trope, and given the shorter length of a playthrough, the randomness and surprises feel crucial.
Paradox says it's aiming to make Afterworld its most accessible grand strategy game, but at this point it's hard to see. This is largely down to the build being alpha. The UI is still in flux and is missing a lot of the informative tooltips that bless other Paradox games, and it's not yet intuitive. Afterworld lets you do so much, but finding out how to do anything requires a lot of effort.
Combined with the lack of tutorial or any real onboarding, it's impossible to say if Afterworld is going to be accessible or not. Though there is one feature that I think is moving things in the right direction, and that's the tech tree.
Instead of seeing the whole tree laid out before you, or getting a random selection of techs to choose from as you do in Stellaris, the tree is revealed through exploration. If your tribe encounters a river, you'll learn about irrigation, unlocking the appropriate idea in the tree. If you meet another tribe and they've established a religion, then you'll discover the organised religion idea.
(Image credit: Paradox) The system also benefits from the map's procedural generation. While the terrain and geography are immutable, you'll encounter different tribes, resources and dangers when you start a new run. So you'll always be able to find that river and unlock irrigation, but other experiences will be random. Just because you've discovered something, however, it doesn't mean you can start researching it.
I wanted to turn mutated trees into steel, for instance, and had discovered the forestry tech tree, but I couldn't start researching the technology without passing a law regarding the exploitation of our forests—which I couldn't do because the council was largely opposed to switching from hunting to logging. Bribes, promises and threats couldn't net me enough support. But then came a rebellion, some upheaval and some new blood at the top of the political hierarchy, and the new folk liked my ideas a lot more.
Yes, you can be a real prick in Afterworld.
Not being able to do stuff because of council opposition was frustrating, but I do love the law system. It's another example of Afterworld doing exciting things at a granular level. If you want your tribe to be clearheaded, for instance, you can ban all intoxicants—or you can ban them for everyone but your slaves, so you can keep them docile. Yes, you can be a real prick in Afterworld.
Embracing a belief system allows you to further define your tribe, and while Afterworld stops short of letting you design a custom religion from scratch, levelling up your belief allows you to select a variety of perks that add new facets to your tribe. Beliefs can also create a lot of welcome friction. Your tribe might include various faiths, which don't always get on, and the faith you've embraced might occasionally be at odds with your laws and goals.
(Image credit: Paradox) Also, yes, you can worship carburetors or books or whatever ancient relics you'll find in the wasteland, or they can be given to bands to increase their standing within the tribe. Some of them even have a practical use beyond using them to exploit the faithful.
Afterworld boasts some of Paradox's most interesting systems, and it's left me genuinely excited to watch it develop. But I don't think the team has quite found the fun yet. It's fascinating and ambitious and often feels like an entirely different approach to grand strategy, but I've spent most of my time with it just troubleshooting and getting lost—in ways that are more frustrating than satisfying.
But even as I've been playing, Paradox has been tweaking. With the feedback the studio has been getting from press and content creators—some of them putting over 100 hours into it already—the devs have a lot to work with now. So there's reason for some optimism. And, importantly, there's already so much good stuff in here.

title: No Half-Life 3 for the Steam Frame, so it looks like this six-year-old game might be the key launch offering instead
text:
Folks who pick up Valve's soon to be released VR headset, the Steam Frame , may get a free Half-Life game with their purchase. Unfortunately, I'm not talking about a brand new release. Plus, it may well be a game virtual reality gamers already have— Half-Life: Alyx .
Dataminer Brad Lynch unearthed this tidbit, sharing a screenshot of code strings that refer to a 'Frame Alyx Promo'. He also observed on X that Valve did a similar thing in the past, offering the game for free with purchases of the Index VR headset after the game launched. That all occurred, of course, quite a few years ago now.
Lynch also noted in an earlier post that internal branches of Alyx had been regularly updated since early last year, though "the public app is only just now starting to get those many months of staged updates." The implication is that these are optimisation tweaks specifically for the Steam Frame, though that's not been confirmed.
Lynch is fairly reliable as a leaker regarding all things VR, having previously spotted that a number of SteamVR code components had been renamed 'Frames' shortly before the Steam Frame was fully revealed.
More recently, he spotted " the first 'official' Android app on Steam ," which would make the most of all of Valve's work on its custom Android compatibility container for Linux, Lepton . Lynch also suggested back in June that the entire VR sphere may enjoy much better displays in the next few years, like Micro-OLEDs from Samsung.
Valve is setting up the system that gives away of copy of Half-Life Alyx to everyone who purchases a Steam Frame 🤔(They did the same thing for those who bought a Valve Index) https://t.co/WaDWKc9Co9 pic.twitter.com/fDQVbX3VBE September 1, 2026
So, no, it doesn't seem that Half-Life 3 is on the horizon, but I won't turn down a free copy of one of the best virtual reality games to come out in years. Mind you, the fact Alyx itself is already six years old probably says a lot about the state of VR these days.
While the Steam Frame is designed to play your entire non-VR library as well, given the lack of big releases in the niche, I personally won't be rushing out to buy a fresh virtual reality headset any time soon.

title: Dwarf Fortress creator says we have a natural lean towards human-made stories, 'but we're all going to be very sorely tested in the coming years' by AI
text:
Dwarf Fortress has an endless capacity for telling stories. It's a game built on procedural generation, and any longtime player'll be able to spin up a dozen yarns about some absurd thing that happened to their gaggle of miners.
Just look at a headline from our own Lincoln Carpenter : "Dwarf Fortress forensic specialists blame mysterious case of spontaneous human combustion on a historical artifact that suddenly remembered it's four times hotter than the surface of the sun." What a beauty.
Anyway, this sort of puts the lie to the idea that generative AI will be the first advent of something that can tell infinite stories, always and forever—because Dwarf Fortress has been doing that without a single LLM for its entire existence. Point being, if you want something that can tell infinite stories, you're probably best off giving us the tools to do that, rather than the finished product itself.
Speaking to PC Gamer's Joshua Wolens at Gamescom 2026 , co-creator Tarn Adams gets a little into it while talking about how they decide whether a simulation's worth it to layer on top of the game: "If you feel like you've played through it yourself a bunch, and you're like, 'oh, that was cool. That's a good beat,' and you're seeing a little narrative forming? Then you know it's going to work."
Adams talks about a hypothetical in which a meeting of dwarven barristers is interrupted by a very rude dog that comes in and bites someone—not even particularly strange, by Dwarf Fortress standards. Asking him as to why we find these emergent, mechanics-based stories so endearing (as opposed to AI slop, which hasn't yet produced a notable story people seem to like), Adams responds:
"Well, I mean, [you like human stories] because you're a human, and you resonate with things that other humans have done because there's a common experience at just the barest basic level.
"You can't always tell," Adams admits. "And that's part of the trick, right? That's what a Turing style test is, right? Can you tell the human spark that's in there? And when you fail a Turing Test as a human, meaning that you got confused by a robot … maybe that's credit to the robot, or maybe that's discredit to you. I don't know which one, but we're all going to be very sorely tested in the coming years as we're surrounded by such matter."
It's an interesting way to look at a Turing Test—not whether a computer can act as intelligently as a human, but whether a computer can replicate our "human spark". Which, at the risk of sounding sentimental, does feel like a vital part to actually enjoying art.
Speaking personally, a large part of why AI art or stories don't interest me isn't necessarily in the technical proficiency of what's happening—it's because I'm interested in learning about a person's worldview, their tastes, their likes and dislikes, their hopes for the future, and having those hopes stirred in myself. The fact a person made something causes it to be more interesting to me.
Which I suppose is why the proc-gen stories of Dwarf Fortress are interesting, because there's a human touch in how the random, computer-generated narratives are described. If you just rattled off a list of events, you'd bore me half to death. But phrase it like Lincoln did above, and I'm having a sensible guffaw—these silly little dwarves shall make writers out of us all.
